title: Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543–1616) — Child Hostage, the Scowling Portrait, Sekigahara, and the Shogunate

teenKit.tldr: A four-year-old heir is sold for pocket change and held hostage to bend his father to a warlord's will—only for his father to call the bluff, proving that in high-stakes politics, a threat only has power if you refuse to let it break you.
teenKit.whyItMatters: It exposes the brutal reality of leverage and game theory, showing how people in power calculate human value versus strategic survival.
keyTakeaways: Betrayal can come from your own family when desperate political deals are struck behind closed doors.
A hostage loses all bargaining power the second the opposing side refuses to flinch at their execution.
True survival in ruthless environments requires mastering the art of patience, concealment, and emotional detachment.

vocab.meaning: A formal, legally binding pledge of loyalty to a lord or ruler.
Using something of value—or someone's life—as tactical pressure to force them to do what you want.
The skillful, often ruthless management of government and international politics.
A final, non-negotiable demand backed by a severe threat if it is rejected.

quiz.question: What happened to the four-year-old boy instead of being safely delivered to the Imagawa clan?
options: He was returned home safely by his grandfather.

quiz.explanation: His grandfather cut a backroom deal, selling him out for pocket change and diverting him straight into enemy hands.

quiz.question: How did the boy's father respond to the Oda clan's threat to execute his son?
options: He immediately surrendered and swore total loyalty.
He sent a massive ransom to buy his son back.
He wrote back saying executing a child proves nothing and refused to break his oath.
He attacked the Oda stronghold with a surprise army.
quiz.explanation: The father called their bluff with cold calculus, declaring that killing a child proves nothing and leaving his oath unbroken.

quiz.question: Why did the Oda warlord ultimately decide not to kill the young hostage?
options: He grew a conscience and felt bad for the kid.
The boy's mother snuck into the camp and rescued him.
A captive loses all leverage and strategic value once the threat of execution is ignored.
The father paid a secret bribe to keep him alive.
quiz.explanation: Once the father refused to trade his loyalty, the hostage lost his leverage, so the warlord kept him locked away instead of killing him.
